doc: Resolving a served `ClientPolicy` (ADR-053) against the shipped defaults. This is the one rule in the kernel whose input comes from the network rather than from a feed, which is what the rows below are mostly about: every field is optional because a partial policy is legal, the document may be missing entirely (a cold start, or offline), and a value that is not a positive finite number is a misconfiguration rather than an aggressive setting — each of those blanks something a rider needs, so it falls back to a number we know works. A port that spread the served object over the defaults instead of filling field by field would pass the first two rows and fail every row after them.

resolveClientPolicy.doc: A served policy document filled out to six usable numbers. `served: null` is the absent document; an absent *field* is an unstated knob. The defaults are pinned here as literal expectations on purpose — they are the shipped values, and a port that transcribed one wrong would otherwise show a rider a different app until its first policy fetch landed.

cases.name: no-policy-at-all
cases.why: The ordinary state of a cold start, and of every offline launch before one has ever been fetched. Must produce the full shipped default set, never a partial object with holes in it — a caller reads six numbers or the screen has no cap.

cases.name: an-empty-document-is-a-valid-policy
cases.why: Distinct from the row above and worth its own row: the fetch SUCCEEDED and the server chose to state nothing. Identical result, different cause, and a port that treated `{}` as an error would break the deploy where we deliberately stop overriding a knob.

cases.name: every-knob-overridden
cases.why: The whole point of the endpoint: six deployed numbers, none of them the default, all of them honoured. If this row passes and the two above pass, the fill is field-by-field rather than positional.

cases.name: one-knob-overridden-the-rest-default
cases.why: The shape a real deploy takes — move one threshold, say nothing about the other five. This is why the fill cannot be `served ?? defaults` at the document level: that would discard five values to change one.

cases.name: zero-is-a-misconfiguration-not-a-setting
cases.why: `maxRows: 0` empties every stop card and `refreshAfterMs: 0` is a request loop. Neither is a policy anybody would deploy on purpose, and both are silent — the app simply looks broken. So a non-positive value is rejected in favour of the default rather than obeyed. Note this is a REJECTION, not a clamp: we do not invent a policy nobody wrote.

cases.name: a-negative-duration-is-rejected
cases.why: The sign error a units mistake produces. Pinned next to the zero row because the pair is the whole guard, and because a port that wrote `value < 0` instead of `value <= 0` passes this row and fails the one above it.

cases.name: a-valid-override-survives-alongside-a-rejected-one
cases.why: A bad knob must not poison the document. One deployed typo would otherwise discard five correct values, turning a small mistake into a total reset — and because the result still looks plausible, nobody would find it.
